summary: Specifies GIST, the General Internet Signalling Transport, which carries signalling messages along the path of a data flow. It is the base protocol of the Next Steps in Signalling (NSIS) framework and uses existing transport and security protocols. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: GIST is a shared transport for signalling messages that travel along the path of a data flow, such as requests to reserve bandwidth or to change a firewall rule. It finds the next node on that path, sends the message to it, and keeps its own state, but leaves the meaning of the message to the application above it.

questions: what is general internet signalling transport
what udp port does gist use
subtitle: The shared transport layer that finds the next signalling node on a flow's path and carries messages to it.

tldr.problem: Applications that must change or watch network state along the path of a data flow all need the same plumbing: find the next signalling-capable node on that path and deliver a message to it.
tldr.mechanism: GIST probes for the next peer with a Query, Response and Confirm handshake sent along the flow's path, then carries messages hop by hop, using UDP for small ones and a TCP connection, optionally with TLS, for the rest.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an Experimental specification from October 2010 that supplies the base protocol of the NSIS framework. The signalling application keeps its own state, and the RFC documents deployment problems with Router Alert Options that its authors expected to be worked around in the field.

today:
RFC 5971 is an Experimental specification, published in October 2010 for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation, and it is not on the Internet Standards Track. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

The RFC's own appendix records what the authors saw in the field: routers that block or mishandle the Router Alert Option, which the peer discovery mechanism depends on. The authors offer two workarounds, sending the probe without the option or tunnelling it past a blocking node, and note that a different Q-mode encapsulation would need a specification change.

sections.title: What GIST Does
sections.content:
GIST is the General Internet Signalling Transport, the common transport layer of the NSIS framework (RFC 4080). Signalling means setting up, changing, tearing down, or watching state held in network devices, such as resource reservations, firewall configuration, or the discovery of path properties like available bandwidth.

This RFC concentrates on path-coupled signalling: signalling that controls the network elements located on the path a particular data flow takes. GIST assumes other mechanisms are responsible for routing within the network, so it complements protocols such as RSVP-TE and LDP rather than replacing them.

GIST deliberately does not handle signalling application state. It provides the common functionality of node discovery, message routing and message transport, so that several signalling applications can re-use one piece of plumbing. The application-specific protocols are called NSIS Signalling Layer Protocols (NSLPs), sit above GIST, and are identified by a 16-bit NSLP identifier assigned by IANA.

A path-coupled signalling session usually has more than two participants, since it involves the nodes along the path rather than only the two endpoints. The RFC notes that not every node on the path has to take part, and that supporting GIST and any signalling application costs performance, so flow-level signalling is more likely to be deployed on edge devices than on core routers.
sections.plainLanguage: GIST is the shared layer that carries signalling messages along the path a data flow takes. It finds the next node on that path, routes messages to it, and carries them, but it does not decide what the messages mean.

sections.title: Core Terms
sections.content:
A flow is a set of packets identified by a fixed combination of header fields. Flows are unidirectional, so a two-way conversation counts as a pair of one-way flows. Downstream means the same direction as the data flow, and upstream means the opposite direction.

A GIST node is any node that runs the GIST protocol, whatever signalling applications it supports. The adjacent peer is the next node along the signalling path, in either direction, with which a GIST node interacts explicitly. The node that starts the handshake to find that peer is the querying node; the node that answers the handshake becomes the responding node.

A session is a single application layer exchange of information for which some state is manipulated or monitored. The session identifier (SID) is a 128-bit value that is opaque to GIST. GIST identifies its routing state by the combination of message routing information (MRI), session identifier and NSLP identifier, so two signalling applications working on the same flow keep separate state.

The messaging association is a single connection between two explicitly identified adjacent peers. It is bidirectional, may refer to flows of either direction, and is entirely internal to GIST: signalling applications never see it.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is one direction of a set of packets. GIST links a node to the next GIST node on that flow's path, and it labels each signalling exchange with a 128-bit session identifier so that separate conversations do not get mixed up.

sections.title: Modes, Messaging Associations and Routing Methods
sections.content:
GIST has two internal modes. Datagram mode (D-mode) sends messages between nodes without transport layer state or security protection, which suits small, infrequent messages with modest delay constraints and no security requirement. A special case of D-mode called Query-mode (Q-mode) is used when no routing state for the peer exists. Connection mode (C-mode) handles all other signalling traffic: it can support large messages and channel security, and it provides congestion control.

C-mode can in principle use any stream or message-oriented transport protocol; this RFC defines TCP as the initial choice. It can also employ a transport layer security association, and this RFC defines TLS as the initial choice. The two modes can be mixed along a path, for example D-mode at the edge of the network and C-mode towards the core, which lets shared security associations carry traffic for several flows at once.

The signalling application does not choose the mode. GIST decides from the size of the message and from the transfer attributes the application stated, and that distinction is not visible at the GIST service interface. The state GIST keeps for C-mode towards a peer, including the signalling destination address, protocol and port numbers and the internal configuration, is the messaging association (MA). There may be several associations between two peers, though the usual case is zero or one.

The algorithm that decides which peer a message goes to is pluggable. A message routing method (MRM) defines the routing information carried in the message, the IP-level encapsulation used to probe the network for the next peer, the validation checks applied to those probes, and the mechanisms available for route change detection. GIST defines two methods: the path-coupled MRM, where signalling follows the route of an existing flow, and the Loose-End MRM, used to discover nodes with particular properties in the direction of a given address, for example a NAT on the upstream data path.

Peering is created only by a handshake. A node issues a Query, and the node along the path that decides to answer it becomes the peer; nodes that do not host the signalling application forward the Query transparently.
sections.plainLanguage: GIST sends small messages as plain UDP datagrams and uses a connection, with optional encryption, for large or sensitive messages. A pluggable routing method decides which neighbour on the path receives each message.

sections.title: Message Processing and the Handshake
sections.content:
At the service interface, a signalling application hands GIST a payload that GIST does not interpret, together with the flow description, the session identifier and message transfer attributes: whether the message must be delivered reliably, what security it needs, and hints about local processing. GIST reports the same information back about messages it receives. The interface is presented the same way at every node and does not change when GIST switches modes, so the choice between them stays inside GIST.

Routing state is organised as a table whose rows are the message routing information, the session identifier and the NSLP identifier. Each row holds the peer identity, either a UDP port number for D-mode or a reference to one or more messaging associations for C-mode, and a validity timer. A default timer value of 30 seconds is RECOMMENDED. When the timer expires, the entry must be purged unless it was refreshed. GIST refreshes state by repeating the handshake; a reasonable policy is to refresh when between one half and three quarters of the validity time has passed, at a moment chosen randomly within that interval so that many nodes do not refresh at once.

The handshake has three messages. The Query probes the network for the correct peer. It is sent in Q-mode encapsulation, carries the routing information, the session identifier, the sender's network layer information and a query cookie, and always asks for a reply. The Response comes back, echoes the query cookie, and carries the responder's own network layer information. If a new messaging association is needed, the response also carries a responder cookie and the responder's proposal for the protocol stack. The Confirm completes the exchange: it echoes the responder cookie and the stack proposal, and when a messaging association is being set up it travels over that association and must precede any other message for the same flow.

The responding node may delay installing routing state until the Confirm arrives, which is a defence against denial-of-service attacks: a node that floods Queries with forged source addresses never causes state to be installed. Cookies make this work. The query cookie must change from one handshake to the next, must not be guessable, must be cheap to validate, and must be unique within a handshake; a suitable implementation is a cryptographically strong random number. The responding node may install state after the initial Query instead, but only when its routing state setup policy allows it.

If a Data or Confirm message arrives for routing state that does not exist, the node rejects it with a "No Routing State" error, and the querying node restarts the handshake with a new Query.
sections.plainLanguage: GIST finds the next node with a three-step exchange: a Query goes out along the flow's path, a Response comes back, and a Confirm finishes the setup. The responder can refuse to store any state until the Confirm proves the sender can receive a reply, which stops forged messages from filling up the node.

sections.title: Messages, Objects and Encapsulation
sections.content:
Every GIST message starts with a common header of two 32-bit words and is followed by a sequence of type-length-value objects. The header carries the protocol version, an 8-bit GIST hop count that prevents a message from looping indefinitely, the message length in 32-bit words, the 16-bit NSLP identifier, a 7-bit message type, and four flags: C for context-free, S for source addressing mode, R for reply requested, and E for explicit routing. The objects that follow must appear in a fixed order for the message type, and a message with a missing, duplicate or invalid object is rejected with an "Object Type Error".

The object types are the message routing information, the session identifier, the network layer information, the stack proposal, the stack configuration data, the query cookie, the responder cookie, the NAT traversal object, the NSLP payload, the error data and the Hello identifier. Each object has a 12-bit type and a 12-bit length in 32-bit words, and two leading bits say what to do with an object the receiver does not recognise: reject the whole message, delete the object, or keep it unchanged in any forwarded message.

There are six message types: Query, Response, Confirm, Data, Error and MA-Hello. The Data message carries signalling application data without modifying GIST state. MA-Hello is sent only in C-mode, carries a Hello identifier, and keeps a messaging association open; it can also be used as a diagnostic request and reply.

In D-mode, the message travels in a single UDP datagram. The payload always begins with a 32-bit magic number, 0x4e04bda5, and a datagram without it is dropped silently. Q-mode encapsulation differs in the way IP addresses are chosen, and it must set the Don't Fragment bit in IPv4, because the checks that identify a Q-mode packet look beyond the IP header and a fragmented datagram would not be intercepted correctly. Q-mode messages go to the well-known UDP port 270 allocated by IANA for GIST, and they carry a Router Alert Option, which lets a node decide quickly whether it needs to examine the datagram at all. A node filters on the port, checks the magic number, and forwards anything that fails the check as an ordinary IP datagram.

In C-mode, the message travels inside a stack of protocols that the two peers agreed on. The stack proposal lists the protocol combinations a side supports, for example TLS over TCP, and the stack configuration data carries the options for those protocols, including the TCP port to connect to. The RFC requires support for TCP, and for TLS in conjunction with TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each GIST message has a fixed short header followed by a list of typed objects. Over UDP, the payload starts with a fixed 32-bit marker, so a node can tell a GIST message from other traffic before doing any real work.

sections.title: The Four State Machines
sections.content:
The protocol is specified as four cooperating state machines. The Node machine exists permanently and handles events that cannot be directed to a more specific machine, such as an inbound message for which no routing state exists. It creates the per-flow machines.

The Querying machine exists for each flow and signalling direction where the node is responsible for creating routing state. It has three states: Awaiting Response, Established and Awaiting Refresh. It sends the Query and starts a No_Response timer; when a Response arrives and routing state is created, it moves to Established, where signalling application data flows normally, and it starts a Refresh timer so that the state is renewed before the peer expires it. An Inactive timer records that no signalling traffic is being handled and lets the machine delete itself.

The Responding machine has the same three states, with Awaiting Confirm in place of Awaiting Response. Depending on policy the machine is created when the Query arrives or only when the Confirm arrives; in the second case the node holds no state at all until the Confirm has been validated. While the machine waits, timer-based retransmission of the Response continues.

The messaging association machine has three states: Awaiting Connection, Connected and Idle. While Connected, a SendHello timer keeps MA-Hello messages going so that the peer holds the association open. When the local node no longer needs it, the machine moves to Idle and a NoHello timer purges the association if the peer's hellos stop arriving; real traffic on the association moves it back to Connected.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is written as four cooperating state machines: one for the node, one for each flow it queries, one for each flow it answers, and one for each connection between peers. Timers drive retransmission, refresh and expiry.

sections.title: Route Changes, NATs and Tunnels
sections.content:
When the IP layer reroutes a flow, the signalling state along the old path has to be updated. The right repair depends on the application, so GIST cannot complete it: its job is to detect the change, update its own routing state consistently, and inform the signalling applications at affected nodes.

Five mechanisms can detect a change. A local trigger comes from the forwarding table. An extended trigger comes from a link-state topology database. GIST C-mode monitoring notices connection packets arriving with a different IP TTL or on a different interface. Data plane monitoring is a change in the flow's behaviour reported by the signalling application. GIST probing is the periodic repetition of the discovery exchange that the specification requires of every node, and the changed peer shows up as a change in the network layer information of the response. GIST classifies each routing state item as Bad, Tentative or Good, and reports the status changes to the signalling application.

The path-coupled MRM depends on the Query imitating the data flow closely, because that is what attaches the signalling to the data path. Downstream, the destination address of the Query is the flow destination from the routing information and the source address is the flow source, so that policy routing and load balancing treat it like the real traffic. A node may instead use its own signalling source address, for example for retransmissions, to receive ICMP errors, or to run GIST through an unmodified NAT.

Legacy NATs translate the IP header of the data packets but not the addressing that GIST carries inside its messages, so after the boundary the signalling would describe the wrong flow. The base specification can only detect this and end the signalling path: the receiver compares the IP source address with the interface address given in the message and returns an "Object Type Error" with the "Untranslated Object" subcode. A GIST-aware NAT solves the problem instead. It rewrites the message routing information to match the data flow bindings and adds a NAT-Traversal object that records the translation, which GIST echoes back in its replies.

IP tunnelling is simpler. A packet carrying a GIST message is treated exactly like any other packet with the same addresses, so the message is not recognisable as GIST until it leaves the tunnel. Signalling for the tunnel itself has to be a separate session, started by one of the tunnel endpoints. IPv4 and IPv6 are handled separately: GIST must use the same IP version for Q-mode encapsulated messages as the flow it signals, and rejects a mismatch with an "MRI Validation Failure" error.
sections.plainLanguage: When a route changes, GIST notices, marks the affected state as suspect, and tells the signalling application so it can repair its own state. NATs need special handling: an ordinary NAT rewrites addresses in the IP header only, so GIST detects that case and stops, while a GIST-aware NAT rewrites the addressing inside the message as well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC sets out three problems: protecting signalling content against eavesdropping, modification, injection and replay while it is in transit; keeping signalling state consistent with the routing of the data flow; and preventing denial-of-service attacks that exhaust a node's state storage, processing power or bandwidth.

GIST has no authentication capability of its own. Peer authentication is delegated to the security protocol inside the messaging association, which for this RFC is TLS. The RFC states that mutual authentication is needed to meet its requirements, but notes that TLS may be used with only a server certificate, in which case the responding node cannot verify the identity of the querying node and cannot rule out a man in the middle. One-sided authentication is described as a transitional stage rather than a robust security solution.

Routing state is protected in four ways. Filtering rejects messages whose flow source addresses could be ruled out by ingress filtering. Return routability checking refuses to install upstream state until the Confirm echoes the responder cookie. Authorisation compares the peer's authenticated identity against a local database of authorised peers, whose entries carry an identity, the namespace it comes from, the scope it applies to and whether it is allowed or denied. SID segregation makes the routing state lookup depend on the session identifier, so a node that wants to overwrite state has to guess it; signalling applications must choose session identifiers that are cryptographically random.

Against flooding, a node may wait for the Confirm before installing any state, and the cookie in the Response is repeated in the Confirm, so state is created only for messages carrying a valid cookie. The added delay is 1.5 node-to-node round-trip times. A single rate limiter applies to all locally generated D-mode traffic, and a token bucket is RECOMMENDED, sized so that the mean output rate is no more than 5 percent of the node's lowest-speed interface.

The security protocol is chosen during the handshake, which opens a downgrade attack in which a node in the middle edits the offered capabilities so that both peers settle for weaker protection. The defence has two parts. The response does not depend on the proposal in the query, so editing the query has no effect on the resulting configuration. The responder's own proposal is echoed in the Confirm, so the responder can check that the querying node received the proposal it made; this only works if the Confirm carries at least integrity protection that cannot be broken in real time.

The remaining threats are listed at the end. An on-path attacker that intercepts the initial Query can do most of what it wants to the later signalling, and the querying node has no assurance that the node beyond the responder is on the path or that the responder has not changed the flow description. Those are left to the signalling application, which can add higher layer protection of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: GIST relies on the security protocol in its connection for authentication and privacy, and adds its own checks to make sure a message came from the node that really sits on the path. Session identifiers are random, so a stranger cannot guess one and take over a session.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
This RFC asks IANA for the well-known UDP port 270 as the destination for Q-mode encapsulated GIST messages, and it creates several registries.

  • NSLP identifiers: a 16-bit value naming the signalling application. Value 0 is used for GIST messages that are not related to any signalling application. Values 1 to 32703 are unassigned, 32704 to 32767 are for private or experimental use, and 32768 to 65536 are reserved. Every NSLPID that uses an MRM requiring a Router Alert Option must be associated with a Router Alert value.
  • GIST message type: a 7-bit field. Values 0 to 5 are Query, Response, Confirm, Data, Error and MA-Hello. Values 6 to 55 are unassigned, 56 to 63 are for private or experimental use, and 64 to 127 are reserved.
  • Object types: a 12-bit field. Values 0 to 10 name the message routing information, session identifier, network layer information, stack proposal, stack configuration data, query cookie, responder cookie, NAT traversal, NSLP data, error and Hello identifier objects.
  • Message routing methods: an 8-bit value. Value 0 is the path-coupled method and value 1 is the Loose-End method.
  • Messaging association protocol identifiers: a 1-byte value. Value 1 is TCP opened in the forwards direction, and value 2 is TLS initiated in the forwards direction. These are tags of their own, not IP protocol numbers, because TLS has no IP protocol number.

Error reporting uses a 2-byte error code with a 1-byte subcode. The RFC defines twelve errors: common header parse error, hop limit exceeded, incorrect encapsulation, incorrectly delivered message, no routing state, unknown NSLPID, endpoint found, message too large, object type error, object value error, invalid IP-layer TTL and MRI validation failure. Each error also carries a class, one of informational, success, protocol error, transient failure or permanent failure.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the registries GIST needs: the port number, the identifiers for signalling applications, the message types, the object types, the routing methods, and the protocols that can be used for a connection.

sections.title: Deployment Issues with Router Alert Options
sections.content:
Peer discovery depends on routers intercepting the Q-mode encapsulated packets, and that interception relies on the Router Alert Option. The RFC describes two practical problems with it.

For IPv4, the Router Alert Option is defined with a 2-byte value field in which only the value zero is defined, and there is no IANA registry for further allocations. The specification says unknown values should be ignored and the packets forwarded as normal IP traffic, but some existing implementations ignore the value field completely and process any packet carrying the option as though the value were zero. A non-zero value therefore cannot be relied upon to keep GIST traffic transparent.

What happens next depends on the node. A router whose closer examination finds no reason to act forwards the packet, which is what the analysis of open-source operating system source code and direct experiments with commercial routers showed. Some other implementations identify the packet as UDP and deliver it to the local UDP stack, where it is dropped or rejected because nothing listens on the GIST port. Either way, Q-mode packets can be blocked in the network, and GIST then does not work there.

The RFC gives two ways around this. A node can be configured to send Q-mode packets without the option at all, but only where it is known that the nodes on the path are able to intercept such packets. Or a node that can identify where the packets are blocked, or that can find a point beyond the blockage, can send them there inside IP-in-IP tunnelling with no option, which skips the input processing of the blocking node and picks up normal GIST behaviour beyond it.

For IPv6 the situation differs, since non-zero Router Alert values are well established and an IANA registry exists. The problem there is immaturity: some implementations treat any packet carrying the option as though it were for local processing, without further analysis. The RFC argues that this prevents any use of the option in such a network, and assumes that such implementations will be fixed as part of the general deployment of IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: GIST's discovery depends on routers inspecting packets that carry a Router Alert Option, and some routers either block those packets or grab them for themselves. The RFC describes two ways to work around this, and notes that the problem is bigger in IPv4 than in IPv6.

layers.label: Signalling applications (NSLPs)
layers.detail: Application-specific protocols that decide what the messages mean

layers.label: GIST
layers.detail: Node discovery, message routing and message transport

layers.label: TLS or DTLS
layers.detail: Optional channel security inside a messaging association

layers.label: UDP, TCP, SCTP, DCCP
layers.detail: Transport protocols; this RFC defines TCP and UDP

layers.label: IP layer security
layers.detail: Optional protection below the transport layer

messages.label: QUERY
messages.note: Q-mode probe along the flow's path, carrying the session identifier, network layer information and a query cookie. The reply flag is always set.

messages.label: RESPONSE
messages.note: Echoes the query cookie and carries the responder's network layer information. With a responder cookie and a stack proposal when a messaging association is being set up.

messages.label: CONFIRM
messages.note: Echoes the responder cookie and the stack proposal. Sent over the new messaging association when one is being set up.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: GIST protocol version; this specification defines version 1.

fields.name: GIST hops
fields.desc: How many more GIST-aware nodes may still process this message.

fields.name: Message Length
fields.desc: Number of 32-bit words in the message after this header.

fields.name: NSLPID
fields.desc: IANA-assigned identifier of the signalling application.

fields.name: C-flag
fields.desc: Set when the message must be readable without routing state; always set for a Query.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Message type: Query, Response, Confirm, Data, Error or MA-Hello.

fields.name: S-flag
fields.desc: Set when the IP source address is also the signalling source address.

fields.name: R-flag
fields.desc: Set when a reply is requested; always set in a Query.

fields.name: E-flag
fields.desc: Set when the message was explicitly routed; only allowed in a Data message.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved bits, set to zero on transmission and ignored on reception.

items.label: Query
items.desc: Probes for the next peer; always sent in Q-mode encapsulation.

items.label: Response
items.desc: Answers a Query and echoes the query cookie.

items.label: Confirm
items.desc: Completes the handshake and echoes the responder cookie.

items.label: Data
items.desc: Carries signalling application data without changing GIST state.

items.label: Error
items.desc: Reports a problem found at the GIST level.

items.label: MA-Hello
items.desc: Keeps a messaging association alive; sent only in C-mode.

items.title: Local trigger
items.text: The forwarding table shows that the next hop changed.

items.title: Extended trigger
items.text: A link-state topology database shows that the path changed.

items.title: C-mode monitoring
items.text: Connection packets arrive with a different IP TTL or on a different interface.

items.title: Data plane monitoring
items.text: The signalling application reports that the behaviour of the flow changed.

items.title: GIST probing
items.text: The repeated discovery exchange reveals a changed peer.
